# From session history to provider requests {#sec:message-formats}

In plain terms: the conversation *is* the product. Everything the model
knows about your project arrives through it — your prompts, the model's
replies, every tool call and tool result — and because the context window is
all the model ever sees, this one list is its entire world. The agent loop's
whole job is growing the conversation one turn at a time.

Pi treats that conversation as its single source of truth. One durable,
append-only record on disk owns the history; every other copy — the runtime
transcript the loop works on, each request sent to a provider — is derived
from it and can be rebuilt at any time.

That one list lives in several places at once, and each place needs a
different shape of it. Each re-expression is a **representation**: the same
conversation, shaped for one layer of the system. This chapter maps the
representations and the functions that carry the conversation across.

This chapter answers three questions:

1. **Why does Pi keep its own message format at all**, instead of storing and
   passing around, say, OpenAI's format? (Answered in [Why Pi has its own
   message representation](#sec:why-canonical), after the walk, where the
   evidence is.)
2. **What does each representation look like?** We will read the actual
   TypeScript types — no guessing what a "message" is.
3. **Which function performs each conversion?** Every boundary has exactly
   one, and knowing them tells you where to hook in as an extension author.

Questions 2 and 3 are answered together as we walk the pipeline from disk to
provider and back — the section headings after [Six representations, one
conversation](#sec:six-representations) *are* the walk. One note on how to
read them: the walk is the spine, six boundary sections in pipeline order.
Tables and the master map are references — revisit them, don't memorize
them. Each boundary section opens with a summary block; the details follow.

## Prerequisites

Read [Sessions, trees, and
compaction](03-sessions-trees-compaction.qmd#sec:sessions) and
[Architecture](05-architecture-for-extensions.qmd#sec:architecture) first: you
should know what a session entry is, what the leaf pointer does, and which
package owns which layer. Terminology is in the
[glossary](20-glossary.qmd#sec:glossary).

Every path below is relative to the Pi monorepo root. The chapter is grounded
in four files and a directory:

- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts` — the session file and
  context reconstruction.
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts` — app-specific message kinds
  and the `convertToLlm()` projection.
- `packages/agent/src/types.ts` — the agent loop's `AgentMessage` type.
- `packages/ai/src/types.ts` — the canonical `Message`, `Context`, and
  `AssistantMessageEvent` types.
- `packages/ai/src/api/` — one adapter per provider API, plus the shared
  `transform-messages.ts`.

## A conversation to carry through the chapter

Abstract pipelines are hard to hold in your head, so we will follow one
concrete exchange from disk to provider and back. You run `pi` and type:

> Read README.md and summarize it in one sentence.

The model calls the `read` tool, Pi executes it and returns the file
contents, and the model answers with a summary. That exchange produces a
conversation with this basic structure — the same structure in every
representation we will meet:

1. A **user message**: your prompt text.
2. An **assistant message**: not plain text, but a request to call `read`
   with `{"path": "README.md"}` — a *tool call*.
3. A **tool result message**: the file contents, answering that tool call.
4. A second **assistant message**: the one-sentence summary.

Here is that conversation at a glance, as Pi is about to send it to the
provider. Throughout this chapter, indented outlines like this one show
nesting — which object contains which — with values sketched, not literal:

```text
Context: one provider request   (you will meet the Context type at Boundary 2)
  systemPrompt: "You are an expert coding assistant ..."
  tools:        [ read, bash, edit, write ]  (name + description + schema)
  messages:
    user        "Read README.md and summarize it ..."
    assistant   content blocks:
                  toolCall   id: call_1, name: read, arguments: {path}
    toolResult  toolCallId: call_1   (answers the call above)
                  content: [ text: "# Pi ..." ]
    assistant   content blocks:
                  text   "README.md introduces the Pi ..."
```

Two structural facts in this picture make everything else in this chapter
click into place:

- **A conversation is a list of messages, and a message is a list of typed
  content blocks.** A message is never just a string. The assistant message
  in step 2 contains a tool-call block; the summary in step 4 contains a text
  block; a single assistant message can hold text, thinking, and several
  tool calls at once. This is why every format below is built from small
  typed blocks rather than raw strings.
- **Every tool call must be answered by exactly one tool result.** The call
  carries an `id`; the result carries a `toolCallId` that equals it — the
  `call_1` pair in the outline. Providers reject transcripts that break this
  pairing with hard errors, so Pi defends it at several layers (you will see
  where).

The outline above is sketched; the artifacts are real. You will see this
exact user message as a line on disk in [The same message in three
shapes](#sec:three-shapes), and the last boundary appends the assistant's
answer as a line just like it.

## Where the conversation lives

Before comparing formats, it helps to see *where* the conversation actually
lives. At any moment, our README.md exchange exists in up to four places at
once — and each place has a different job with conflicting demands, which is
why each keeps the conversation in a different shape. No single shape serves
all four jobs, so Pi re-expresses the conversation at each boundary — and
each boundary has exactly one converting function.

**On disk: the durable copy.** Every message, tool call, and tool result is
appended to a session file (one JSON object per line, called JSONL) under
`~/.pi/agent/sessions/` (one subdirectory per project). This copy's job is
**durability**: it must survive restarts and crashes, power `/resume` next
week, and keep abandoned branches for `/tree`. It is the only copy that owns
history — the others are derived from it and can be rebuilt at any time.

**In memory: the working copy.** While the agent runs, it operates on a plain
in-memory list of message objects. This copy's job is **execution**: the loop
appends to it, the UI renders it, extensions transform it. It exists for one
run and is rebuilt from disk on resume.

**In each request: the per-call copy.** Just before a model call, Pi assembles
a fresh, self-contained request: a system prompt, the selected messages, and
the tool definitions. This copy's job is **economy**: the model gets exactly
what it needs for this call — no branch metadata, no extension state, nothing
that wastes tokens. It is thrown away the moment the call ends and reassembled
from scratch before the next one.

**On the wire: the provider's copy.** The request leaves the process as an
HTTP body, and the answer comes back as a stream of chunks. This copy's job
is **obedience**: its shape is dictated entirely by the provider's API and
lasts exactly one exchange.

| Home | Lifetime | Optimized for |
|---|---|---|
| On disk (session file) | Months; survives restarts | Durability: resume, branch, audit |
| In memory (agent loop) | One run | Execution: append, stream, render |
| In each request | One model call | Economy: exactly what the model needs |
| On the wire (HTTP) | One exchange | Obedience: the provider's rules |

Two things to carry forward. First, these are **projections, not copies** of
one object: a projection keeps some fields and drops others, on purpose —
like a shadow of the full record that preserves exactly what the next layer
needs. Second, the four homes produce the six representations you will meet
below: the request home splits into the message list and its container, and
the wire home splits into the outbound payload and the inbound event stream.
@fig-homes-to-representations makes the mapping explicit — node labels match
the master map (@fig-type-chain) you will meet shortly:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-homes-to-representations
%%| fig-cap: "Four homes, six representations. The request home splits into the message list and its container; the wire home into payload and event stream."
%%| fig-width: 5.6
%%| fig-pos: "H"
flowchart LR
  DISK["on disk<br/>session file"] --> SE["SessionEntry<br/>core/session-manager.ts"]
  MEM["in memory<br/>agent loop"] --> AM["AgentMessage<br/>agent/src/types.ts"]
  REQ["in each request<br/>one model call"] --> MSG["Message<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
  REQ --> CTX["Context<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
  WIRE["on the wire<br/>HTTP"] --> PAY["wire payload<br/>ai/src/api/*.ts"]
  WIRE --> EVT["AssistantMessageEvent<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
```

Three of these homes are Pi's to design; the wire is not. So why doesn't Pi
borrow the provider's format for its own three and skip the conversions
entirely? That is a real option — hold the question. The walk gives you the
evidence, and [Why Pi has its own message
representation](#sec:why-canonical) answers it.

## Six representations, one conversation {#sec:six-representations}

The same conversation exists in these shapes at different moments. Paths are
relative to `packages/` (`core/` means `packages/coding-agent/src/core/`).
Don't memorize these six rows — each gets its own boundary section, and the
walk reintroduces it with an example:

| Representation | Defined in | What it is | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SessionEntry` | `session-manager.ts` | Interface union, serialized as one JSONL line per entry | Durable record: one node of the session tree on disk |
| `AgentMessage` | `agent/src/types.ts` | Type union: canonical `Message` plus app-specific roles | Runtime transcript inside the agent loop |
| `Message` | `ai/src/types.ts` | Type union of `UserMessage`, `AssistantMessage`, `ToolResultMessage` | Pi's provider-neutral canonical format |
| `Context` | `ai/src/types.ts` | Interface (`systemPrompt`, `messages`, `tools`) | One complete provider request, before serialization |
| Wire payload | `ai/src/api/*.ts` | Provider SDK types (e.g. `MessageParam`), serialized as the HTTP body | What a specific provider API actually receives |
| `AssistantMessageEvent` | `ai/src/types.ts` | Type union; one event per streamed chunk | Inbound protocol: one streamed response, normalized |

The conversions between them are where the design lives. Each boundary has
exactly one converting function, and each one adds something the next layer
needs while leaving something behind. @fig-type-chain is the chapter's
master map: nodes are the six representations (each labeled with the file
that defines it), edges are the functions that carry the conversation
across, numbered in the order the rest of the chapter walks them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-type-chain
%%| fig-cap: "The type chain: one conversation carried across six boundaries. Nodes are representations; numbered edges are the one function that crosses that boundary (edges 3 and 4 share an arrow — both run inside the adapter). Edge 5's events arrive on the provider's response stream; edge 6 persists the finished AssistantMessage, not the events."
%%| fig-width: 3.3
%%| fig-pos: "H"
flowchart TD
  SE["SessionEntry<br/>core/session-manager.ts"] -->|"1 · buildSessionContext()"| AM["AgentMessage<br/>agent/src/types.ts"]
  AM -->|"2 · convertToLlm()"| MSG["Message<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
  MSG -->|"request assembly"| CTX["Context<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
  CTX -->|"3 · transformMessages()<br/>4 · adapter convertMessages()"| PAY["wire payload<br/>ai/src/api/*.ts"]
  PAY -->|"5 · adapter event translation"| EVT["AssistantMessageEvent<br/>ai/src/types.ts"]
  EVT -->|"stream resolves to<br/>AssistantMessage"| AM
  AM -->|"6 · appendMessage()<br/>on message_end"| SE
```

One edge is deliberately unnumbered. Request assembly (`Message[] →
Context`) groups fields — it converts nothing, so it gets no boundary block
of its own; the `Context` interface arrives with Boundary 2, where
`convertToLlm()`'s output lands. The section headings ahead *are* this map:
Boundaries 1–6 in order, outbound first, then back. Each crossing opens with
a **boundary block** — the type transition, the exact function and its file,
what the conversion adds, and what it deliberately leaves behind — followed
by a concrete before-and-after from the running example.

## Outbound: from disk to the provider

### Boundary 1 — `SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage` {#sec:boundary-1}

On disk, the same conversation looks like this — one JSON object per line,
appended as the exchange unfolds (a nesting outline; values sketched, not
literal):

```text
session file: one JSON object per line, append-only
  line 1:  header   { type: "session", version: 3, id, cwd }
  line 2:  entry    { type: "message", id, parentId, timestamp,
                      message: <the user message> }
  line 3:  entry    { type: "message", id, parentId, timestamp,
                      message: <assistant with the toolCall> }
  line 4:  entry    { type: "message", id, parentId, timestamp,
                      message: <the toolResult> }
  line 5:  entry    { type: "message", id, parentId, timestamp,
                      message: <assistant summary> }
```

The nesting is one level deeper than in the request: the file wraps every
message in an **entry envelope** (`id`, `parentId`, `timestamp`), and it
interleaves non-message entries (settings changes, labels, extension state)
that never become context.

**Parsing, tolerant by design.** The first line must be the `type: "session"`
header; older files are migrated in place to the current version
(`CURRENT_SESSION_VERSION = 3`; version 2 added the `id`/`parentId` tree
structure, version 3 renamed the old `hookMessage` role to `custom`).
`SessionManager` reads the file in chunks and `JSON.parse`s each line;
**malformed lines are skipped, not fatal**. The why: the file is an
append-only log, and appends can be torn — a crash or a `kill` can leave a
half-written final line. Tolerating that line is what keeps a crashed
session resumable instead of unreadable. The practical rule: read sessions
through `SessionManager`, never by assuming every line parses or matches the
newest version.

Every entry after the header shares the same base shape, and the file's
lines are typed as a union over the header and all entry kinds
(`session-manager.ts`):

```ts
/** Raw file entry (includes header) */
export type FileEntry = SessionHeader | SessionEntry;

export type SessionEntry =
	| SessionMessageEntry
	| ThinkingLevelChangeEntry
	| ModelChangeEntry
	| CompactionEntry
	| BranchSummaryEntry
	| CustomEntry
	| CustomMessageEntry
	| LabelEntry
	| SessionInfoEntry;

export interface SessionEntryBase {
	type: string;
	id: string;
	parentId: string | null;
	timestamp: string;
}
```

`id` and `parentId` are tree links: every entry points at its parent, which
is what lets one file hold several continuations of the same conversation.

::: {.callout-note}
## Recap from chapter 03
The file is append-only, but the *active conversation* is not "all lines in
order": a flat array cannot hold two answers to the same prompt.
`SessionManager` keeps a **leaf pointer**; context construction walks
`parentId` links from the leaf to the root and reverses the result
(`buildSessionPath()`), so entries on abandoned branches stay in the file
but never reach the model. On top of that path, `buildContextEntries()`
applies compaction: the latest `compaction` entry is kept as an entry of its
own, the summarized span before it is dropped, and entries from
`firstKeptEntryId` onward are retained. Nothing is deleted from the file —
compaction is a projection, not an edit. The full mechanics are in
[Sessions, trees, and
compaction](03-sessions-trees-compaction.qmd#sec:sessions).
:::

**Boundary 1 of 6 — `SessionEntry[]` → `AgentMessage[]`** (edge 1 in
@fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* **`SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage`** → `Message` → `Context` →
wire payload → `AssistantMessageEvent` → (back to) `SessionEntry`.

```ts
export function buildSessionContext(
	entries: SessionEntry[],
	leafId?: string | null,
	byId?: Map<string, SessionEntry>,
): SessionContext;

export function sessionEntryToContextMessages(entry: SessionEntry): AgentMessage[];
```

Both in `packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts`.
**Adds:** branch selection, compaction substitution, current settings.
**Leaves behind:** abandoned branches, durable-only entries.

`sessionEntryToContextMessages()` converts one selected entry into zero or
more `AgentMessage`s. This is the first place the "not everything becomes
context" rule is enforced:

| Entry `type` | Becomes model context? | Projection |
|---|---|---|
| `message` | Yes | The stored `AgentMessage` passes through (null content repaired to `[]`) |
| `custom_message` | Yes | Converted to a `CustomMessage` via `createCustomMessage()` |
| `compaction` | Yes | Converted to a `CompactionSummaryMessage` |
| `branch_summary` | Yes | Converted to a `BranchSummaryMessage` (when a summary exists) |
| `thinking_level_change` | No | Restores loop state (thinking level), not a message |
| `model_change` | No | Restores loop state (model selection), not a message |
| `custom` | No | Durable extension state only (`pi.appendEntry()`); ignored here |
| `label` | No | Bookmark metadata for `/tree` |
| `session_info` | No | Display-name metadata |

The zero-message rows are concrete, not hypothetical. An extension's durable
state entry sits in the file like any other line:

```json
{
  "type": "custom",
  "id": "8c1f0a2b",
  "parentId": "3f9a1c82",
  "timestamp": "2025-07-13T15:22:12.100Z",
  "customType": "my-extension.state",
  "data": { "lastRun": 1752420062000 }
}
```

`sessionEntryToContextMessages()` returns an empty array for it: the entry
survives `/resume` and `/tree`, and never costs a token of model context.

`buildSessionContext()` ties it together: it walks the path to recover the
current thinking level and model, then flat-maps the compaction-aware entry
list through `sessionEntryToContextMessages()`. The result is:

```ts
export interface SessionContext {
	messages: AgentMessage[];
	thinkingLevel: string;
	model: { provider: string; modelId: string } | null;
}
```

Note what just happened: nine entry kinds collapsed into messages plus two
settings. An extension's private `custom` entries survive resume and `/tree`
without ever reaching the model.

### Boundary 2 — `AgentMessage` → `Message` {#sec:boundary-2}

**Boundary 2 of 6 — `AgentMessage[]` → `Message[]`** (edge 2 in
@fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* `SessionEntry` → **`AgentMessage` → `Message`** → `Context` →
wire payload → `AssistantMessageEvent` → (back to) `SessionEntry`.

```ts
export function convertToLlm(messages: AgentMessage[]): Message[];
```

`packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts`.
**Adds:** canonical roles for app-specific messages.
**Leaves behind:** excluded bash runs, unknown kinds.

The agent loop never converts messages itself; `AgentLoopConfig.convertToLlm`
is a required callback (`packages/agent/src/types.ts`):

```ts
convertToLlm: (messages: AgentMessage[]) => Message[] | Promise<Message[]>;
```

The why: this keeps `packages/agent` app-agnostic — the loop orchestrates
prompts, tools, and events without knowing that bash executions or
compaction summaries exist. Coding-agent wires the callback to
`convertToLlm()` in `core/messages.ts` (wrapped in `core/sdk.ts` to replace
images with a placeholder when image reading is disabled).

**The input side.** `AgentMessage` is the canonical `Message` union plus
whatever an application registers on the `CustomAgentMessages` interface —
empty by default, so apps can extend it via *declaration merging*
(TypeScript's way of letting another package add members to an interface —
`packages/agent` stays generic while the coding agent registers its own
roles):

```ts
// packages/agent/src/types.ts
export interface CustomAgentMessages {
	// Empty by default - apps extend via declaration merging
}

export type AgentMessage = Message | CustomAgentMessages[keyof CustomAgentMessages];

// packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts
declare module "@earendil-works/pi-agent-core" {
	interface CustomAgentMessages {
		bashExecution: BashExecutionMessage;
		custom: CustomMessage;
		branchSummary: BranchSummaryMessage;
		compactionSummary: CompactionSummaryMessage;
	}
}
```

So inside the coding agent, an `AgentMessage` is any canonical message, or a
`bashExecution` (a bash run: command, output, exitCode), a `custom` message
(extension-injected), a `branchSummary`, or a `compactionSummary`. The
provider layer must not know about any of that.

**The output side.** Pi's exchange format is the smaller `Message` union in
`packages/ai/src/types.ts` — three roles, each a plain interface:

```ts
export type Message = UserMessage | AssistantMessage | ToolResultMessage;

export interface UserMessage {
	role: "user";
	content: string | (TextContent | ImageContent)[];
	timestamp: number; // Unix timestamp in milliseconds
}

export interface AssistantMessage {
	role: "assistant";
	content: (TextContent | ThinkingContent | ToolCall)[];
	api: Api;
	provider: ProviderId;
	model: string;
	responseModel?: string;
	responseId?: string;
	diagnostics?: AssistantMessageDiagnostic[];
	usage: Usage;
	stopReason: StopReason;
	errorMessage?: string;
	timestamp: number; // Unix timestamp in milliseconds
}

export interface ToolResultMessage<TDetails = any> {
	role: "toolResult";
	toolCallId: string;
	toolName: string;
	content: (TextContent | ImageContent)[];
	details?: TDetails;
	usage?: Usage;
	addedToolNames?: string[];
	isError: boolean;
	timestamp: number; // Unix timestamp in milliseconds
}
```

The content blocks are **discriminated unions** — a union where every
variant carries a shared literal field you can `switch` on. Here every block
has a `type` field, so a `switch` on `block.type` is exhaustive:

```ts
export type StopReason = "stop" | "length" | "toolUse" | "error" | "aborted";

export interface TextContent {
	type: "text";
	text: string;
	textSignature?: string;
}

export interface ThinkingContent {
	type: "thinking";
	thinking: string;
	thinkingSignature?: string;
	redacted?: boolean;
}

export interface ImageContent {
	type: "image";
	data: string; // base64 encoded image data
	mimeType: string;
}

export interface ToolCall {
	type: "toolCall";
	id: string;
	name: string;
	arguments: Record<string, any>;
	thoughtSignature?: string;
}
```

Three semantic details the signatures only hint at: `thinkingSignature`
carries an opaque token so reasoning can be replayed to the same model;
`errorMessage` is set on the `"error"` and `"aborted"` stop reasons; and
`details` on a tool result holds structured data for UI rendering that never
affects the model. This is why the format can stay provider-neutral:
reasoning, images, and tool calls are first-class blocks, not
provider-specific JSON fragments.

The design pays off directly in the tool-call invariant from the running
example: **every `ToolCall` block's `id` must be answered by a
`ToolResultMessage` whose `toolCallId` equals it.** Providers enforce this
pairing with hard errors, and Pi enforces it itself in `transformMessages()`
(Boundary 3), which inserts synthetic `"No result provided"` error results
for orphaned calls rather than send an invalid transcript.

**The running example, canonical.** Here is the entire exchange in this
format — the complete canonical `Message[]` (real assistant messages
additionally carry `api`, `provider`, `model`, and `usage`; omitted here so
the structure stands out):

```json
[
  {
    "role": "user",
    "content": "Read README.md and summarize it in one sentence.",
    "timestamp": 1752420131000
  },
  {
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": [
      {
        "type": "toolCall",
        "id": "call_1",
        "name": "read",
        "arguments": { "path": "README.md" }
      }
    ],
    "stopReason": "toolUse",
    "timestamp": 1752420134000
  },
  {
    "role": "toolResult",
    "toolCallId": "call_1",
    "toolName": "read",
    "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "# Pi\n..." }],
    "isError": false,
    "timestamp": 1752420135000
  },
  {
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "README.md introduces the Pi ..." }
    ],
    "stopReason": "stop",
    "timestamp": 1752420139000
  }
]
```

Read it against the four-step structure from earlier: user, assistant tool
call, tool result, assistant answer.

**The projection in action.** `convertToLlm()` is a pure projection:

- `user`, `assistant`, `toolResult` — pass through unchanged.
- `bashExecution` — becomes a user message whose text is
  `bashExecutionToText()`; skipped entirely when `excludeFromContext` is set
  (the `!!` prefix).
- `custom` — becomes a user message from its string or text/image content.
- `branchSummary` / `compactionSummary` — become user messages with the
  summary wrapped in an explanatory prefix/suffix.

Anything else is filtered out. One projection in miniature — a `!`-command
bash run crosses the boundary like this:

```json
{
  "role": "bashExecution",
  "command": "git status --short",
  "output": " M README.md\n",
  "exitCode": 0,
  "cancelled": false,
  "truncated": false,
  "timestamp": 1752420142000
}
```

becomes a plain user message whose text `bashExecutionToText()` renders as a
single text block (the `\n`s are newlines in the real string):

```json
{
  "role": "user",
  "content": [{ "type": "text",
    "text": "Ran `git status --short`\n```\n M README.md\n\n```" }],
  "timestamp": 1752420142000
}
```

A coding-agent-only role the provider layer never learns about, flattened
into text the model reads like any user note.

**The container.** The canonical array lands in a `Context` as `messages` —
exactly one request's worth of canonical state. This is request assembly,
the unnumbered edge on @fig-type-chain: it groups fields, converts nothing:

```ts
export interface Tool<TParameters extends TSchema = TSchema> {
	name: string;
	description: string;
	parameters: TParameters;
	constrainedSampling?: false | ConstrainedSamplingConfig;
}

export interface Context {
	systemPrompt?: string;
	messages: Message[];
	tools?: Tool[];
}
```

`Tool` parameter schemas are written with
[TypeBox](20-glossary.qmd#sec:glossary) (`TSchema`), which keeps them JSON
Schema-compatible for every provider adapter.

::: {.callout-note}
## Data, not classes
None of the message formats are classes. `SessionEntry`, `AgentMessage`,
`Message`, `Context`, and `AssistantMessageEvent` are plain-object interfaces
and type unions — data with no methods. You construct them as object literals
(or with small factories such as `createCompactionSummaryMessage()`), you can
`JSON.stringify` them as-is, and tests build them as fixtures without
instantiating machinery. The only runtime classes in this story are three:
`SessionManager` owns the file, `Agent` owns the running loop, and
`AssistantMessageEventStream` carries the response. There is no `Message`
class to instantiate or subclass.
:::

### The same message in three shapes {#sec:three-shapes}

To see the first two boundaries concretely, here is our example prompt in
its three shapes so far — three of the six representations from [Six
representations, one conversation](#sec:six-representations):
`SessionEntry`, `AgentMessage`, and `Message` sitting inside a `Context`. On
disk, the user message is one line in the session file, wrapped in its entry
envelope (shown pretty-printed; real lines have no whitespace):

```json
{
  "type": "message",
  "id": "3f9a1c82",
  "parentId": "e17b04d6",
  "timestamp": "2025-07-13T15:22:11.421Z",
  "message": {
    "role": "user",
    "content": "Read README.md and summarize it in one sentence.",
    "timestamp": 1752420131000
  }
}
```

Note the two timestamps with two different jobs: the envelope's ISO string
is when the line was appended (durability), the message's Unix milliseconds
are when the message was created. On a fresh session, Pi creates the file
only when the first assistant message lands — so the header, this line, and
the first assistant line appear together; from then on, and on resumed
sessions, every line is appended as it happens.

After `buildSessionContext()` (Boundary 1), the envelope is gone and the
inner object joins the runtime transcript as an `AgentMessage`:

```json
{
  "role": "user",
  "content": "Read README.md and summarize it in one sentence.",
  "timestamp": 1752420131000
}
```

After `convertToLlm()` (Boundary 2) and request assembly, the same message
sits inside a `Context` as a canonical `UserMessage` — structurally
unchanged, because user messages are already canonical:

```json
{
  "systemPrompt": "You are an expert coding assistant ...",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Read README.md and summarize it in one sentence.",
      "timestamp": 1752420131000
    }
  ],
  "tools": [ "..." ]
}
```

Spot the difference across the three shapes: the payload never changes, only
the wrapping. The entry adds tree links and an ISO timestamp for durability;
the runtime and canonical shapes keep only what a model request needs.

### Boundary 3 — `Message` → `Message`, normalized {#sec:boundary-3}

**Boundary 3 of 6 — `Message[]` → `Message[]`, normalized for the target
model** (edge 3 in @fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* `SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage` → `Message` → **`Context` →
wire payload** → `AssistantMessageEvent` → (back to) `SessionEntry`.

```ts
export function transformMessages<TApi extends Api>(
	messages: Message[],
	model: Model<TApi>,
	normalizeToolCallId?: (id: string, model: Model<TApi>, source: AssistantMessage) => string,
): Message[];
```

In `packages/ai/src/api/transform-messages.ts`.
**Adds:** target-model fixups (IDs, images, thinking).
**Leaves behind:** errored turns, cross-model thinking.

Every chat adapter under `packages/ai/src/api/` — except `pi-messages.ts`,
which speaks Pi's own message protocol and sends the canonical `Context`
untransformed — first calls `transformMessages()`, passing the messages, the
target model, and a tool-call-ID normalizer (five adapters reach it through
shared helpers). The why: some fixups depend on the *target* model, not the
source — and every adapter needs the same ones. Doing them once, in a shared
provider-neutral pass, means a new adapter gets them for free:

- Normalizes tool-call IDs when history crosses models (e.g. 450+-character
  OpenAI Responses IDs containing `|` into Anthropic's `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`
  shape with a 64-character limit), remapping matching `toolCallId`s on
  results. (OpenAI's completions adapter uses its own 40-character scheme
  with a hash fallback.)
- Replaces images with a text placeholder when the target model has no
  vision input.
- Replays thinking blocks only for the same model that produced them;
  cross-model, they degrade to plain text or are dropped.
- Skips assistant messages whose `stopReason` is `"error"` or `"aborted"`,
  and inserts synthetic tool results for orphaned tool calls.

The first fixup, concretely — a session that started on OpenAI's Responses
API can carry tool-call IDs Anthropic rejects, so the normalizer rewrites
the ID and every `toolCallId` that references it (IDs abbreviated):

```text
before
  toolCall:    id:         "fc_0c82…|call_7c1d…"   (450+ chars, contains "|")
  toolResult:  toolCallId: "fc_0c82…|call_7c1d…"
after
  toolCall:    id:         "fc_0c82…_call_7c1d…"   ("|" → "_", max 64 chars)
  toolResult:  toolCallId: "fc_0c82…_call_7c1d…"   (remapped to match)
```

### Boundary 4 — `Message` → wire payload {#sec:boundary-4}

**Boundary 4 of 6 — `Message[]` → provider JSON** (edge 4 in
@fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* `SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage` → `Message` → **`Context` →
wire payload** → `AssistantMessageEvent` → (back to) `SessionEntry`.

`convertMessages(transformedMessages, ...)` — one per adapter, private to
its file in `packages/ai/src/api/` (e.g. `anthropic-messages.ts`,
`openai-completions.ts`), with no common signature.
**Adds:** provider roles, field names, encodings.
**Leaves behind:** the provider-neutral shape.

The adapter's own `convertMessages()` turns the normalized `Message[]` into
provider SDK types. This is where the canonical format's neutrality pays
off: one tool-call exchange, two very different wire shapes.

The blocks below zoom into messages 2 and 3 of the canonical array — the
tool call and its result — serialized three ways. Canonical form first
(again with `api`, `provider`, `model`, `usage`, and `stopReason` omitted):

```json
{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "toolCall",
      "id": "call_1",
      "name": "read",
      "arguments": { "path": "README.md" }
    }
  ]
}
{
  "role": "toolResult",
  "toolCallId": "call_1",
  "toolName": "read",
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "# Pi\n..." }],
  "isError": false
}
```

`openai-completions.ts` serializes the exchange as an assistant message
with a `tool_calls` array (arguments **stringified**) followed by a
dedicated `role: "tool"` message keyed by `tool_call_id`:

```json
{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": null,
  "tool_calls": [
    {
      "id": "call_1",
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "read",
        "arguments": "{\"path\":\"README.md\"}"
      }
    }
  ]
}
{
  "role": "tool",
  "tool_call_id": "call_1",
  "content": "# Pi\n..."
}
```

(The assistant `content` is `null` by default; some provider compat profiles
use an empty string instead.)

`anthropic-messages.ts` serializes the same exchange as a `tool_use` content
block (arguments as a structured `input` object), with the result moved into
a **`tool_result` block inside a user-role message**:

```json
{
  "role": "assistant",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "tool_use",
      "id": "call_1",
      "name": "read",
      "input": { "path": "README.md" }
    }
  ]
}
{
  "role": "user",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "tool_result",
      "tool_use_id": "call_1",
      "content": "# Pi\n...",
      "is_error": false
    }
  ]
}
```

(The `tool_result` content is a plain string for text-only results; it
becomes a block array when images are present.)

Put the two side by side and the adapter's job is exact: arguments as string
vs. object, a `tool` role vs. a `user`-wrapped block, `tool_call_id` vs.
`tool_use_id` — three structural differences absorbed entirely by the
adapter. Nothing above `Context` changes, and the session file keeps the
single canonical form regardless of which model is active. Remember the
question parked at the end of the homes section — this side by side is the
evidence; [Models, providers, and
authentication](12-models-providers-and-auth.qmd#sec:models) covers how the
adapter itself is selected.

## Inbound: from the provider back to disk

### Boundary 5 — provider chunks → `AssistantMessageEvent` {#sec:boundary-5}

**Boundary 5 of 6 — provider chunks → `AssistantMessageEvent`** (edge 5 in
@fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* `SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage` → `Message` → `Context` →
**wire payload → `AssistantMessageEvent`** → (back to) `SessionEntry`.

Each adapter's event translation — `packages/ai/src/api/anthropic-messages.ts`
and its siblings — pushing onto an `AssistantMessageEventStream`
(`packages/ai/src/utils/event-stream.ts`).
**Adds:** normalized events, the final `AssistantMessage`.
**Leaves behind:** the provider chunk format.

**Adapter translation.** The adapter consumes the provider's stream (SSE
chunks or WebSocket frames) and pushes normalized `AssistantMessageEvent`s.
The union has twelve variants — one per content-block transition, plus the
two terminal events (`ai/src/types.ts`):

```ts
export type AssistantMessageEvent =
	| { type: "start"; partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "text_start"; contentIndex: number; partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "text_delta"; contentIndex: number; delta: string;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "text_end"; contentIndex: number; content: string;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "thinking_start"; contentIndex: number; partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "thinking_delta"; contentIndex: number; delta: string;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "thinking_end"; contentIndex: number; content: string;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "toolcall_start"; contentIndex: number; partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "toolcall_delta"; contentIndex: number; delta: string;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "toolcall_end"; contentIndex: number; toolCall: ToolCall;
	    partial: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "done"; reason: Extract<StopReason, "stop" | "length" | "toolUse">;
	    message: AssistantMessage }
	| { type: "error"; reason: Extract<StopReason, "aborted" | "error">;
	    error: AssistantMessage };
```

Read the shape of a turn off the union: `start`, then per content block a
`*_start`, `*_delta` chunks, a `*_end`, and finally `done` or `error`. The
start and delta events carry the growing `partial` assistant message, so
consumers never parse provider JSON; the terminal events carry the finished
thing instead — `done` carries the final `message`, `error` carries the
failed message as `error`. Note the `reason` types: a `done` reason is only
ever `stop`, `length`, or `toolUse`; an `error` reason is `aborted` or
`error`.

What the adapter absorbs is concrete — Anthropic streams this chunk (one SSE
event, pretty-printed):

```json
{
  "type": "content_block_delta",
  "index": 0,
  "delta": { "type": "text_delta", "text": "README.md introduces" }
}
```

and pushes this normalized event instead — provider nesting gone, field
names canonical:

```json
{ "type": "text_delta", "contentIndex": 0,
  "delta": "README.md introduces", "partial": "..." }
```

For the summary answer in our example, the full stream looks like this
(`partial` and the final `message` are full assistant-message objects,
trimmed here):

```json
{ "type": "text_start", "contentIndex": 0, "partial": "..." }
{ "type": "text_delta", "contentIndex": 0,
  "delta": "README.md introduces", "partial": "..." }
{ "type": "text_delta", "contentIndex": 0,
  "delta": " the Pi ...", "partial": "..." }
{ "type": "text_end", "contentIndex": 0,
  "content": "README.md introduces the Pi ...", "partial": "..." }
{ "type": "done", "reason": "stop", "message": "..." }
```

**The event stream.** `AssistantMessageEventStream` is the one runtime class
on this path — an async-iterable queue whose `result()` promise resolves to
the final `AssistantMessage` (public surface, bodies elided):

```ts
export class AssistantMessageEventStream
    extends EventStream<AssistantMessageEvent, AssistantMessage> {
	push(event: AssistantMessageEvent): void;   // deliver; done/error also resolve result()
	end(result?: AssistantMessage): void;       // close the stream
	[Symbol.asyncIterator](): AsyncIterator<AssistantMessageEvent>;
	result(): Promise<AssistantMessage>;        // done → event.message; error → event.error
}
```

The stream contract forbids throwing: failures arrive as an `error` event
carrying an assistant message with `stopReason: "error"` (or `"aborted"`)
and `errorMessage` set, and `result()` resolves — never rejects — with that
message. The why: if errors are data, every consumer — the loop, the UI,
persistence — handles success and failure through the same code path, and no
stack unwinding can lose a half-finished turn.

**From stream events to loop events.** Events in Pi exist at two levels.
Inside `packages/ai`, the stream speaks `AssistantMessageEvent` — one per
provider chunk. The agent loop translates those into `AgentEvent`s — the
lifecycle that extensions and the UI subscribe to. `message_update` is the
bridge: it wraps each stream event. The loop iterates the stream with
`for await` and re-emits the union's three nested lifecycles plus tool
execution (`packages/agent/src/types.ts`; the grouping comments are the
source's own):

```ts
export type AgentEvent =
	// Agent lifecycle
	| { type: "agent_start" }
	| { type: "agent_end"; messages: AgentMessage[] }
	// Turn lifecycle - a turn is one assistant response + any tool calls/results
	| { type: "turn_start" }
	| { type: "turn_end"; message: AgentMessage; toolResults: ToolResultMessage[] }
	// Message lifecycle - emitted for user, assistant, and toolResult messages
	| { type: "message_start"; message: AgentMessage }
	// Only emitted for assistant messages during streaming
	| { type: "message_update"; message: AgentMessage;
	    assistantMessageEvent: AssistantMessageEvent }
	| { type: "message_end"; message: AgentMessage }
	// Tool execution lifecycle
	| { type: "tool_execution_start"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string; args: any }
	| { type: "tool_execution_update"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string;
	    args: any; partialResult: any }
	| { type: "tool_execution_end"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string;
	    result: any; isError: boolean };
```

Two facts to read off the union: `message_start` and `message_end` fire for
user, assistant, *and* toolResult messages, while `message_update` fires
only during assistant streaming; and a **turn** is one assistant response
plus any tool calls and results it triggered — so our README exchange is
*two* turns, not one. For our exchange, the loop emits (an outline;
`tool_execution_update` fires only if the tool streams partials, so it may
not appear at all):

```text
agent_start
turn_start                                            (first turn)
  message_start / message_end    (your prompt)
  message_start                  (assistant, on stream start)
  message_update × N             (each wraps an assistantMessageEvent)
  message_end                    (the tool-call message)
  tool_execution_start → tool_execution_end      (read call_1)
  message_start / message_end    (the toolResult)
turn_end   { message: tool-call message, toolResults: [read result] }
turn_start                                            (second turn)
  message_start / message_update × N / message_end   (the summary)
turn_end   { message: summary, toolResults: [] }
agent_end  { messages: [prompt, tool-call msg, toolResult, summary] }
```

`turn_end` carries the turn's own assistant message and its tool results;
`agent_end` carries everything this run added. And because failures arrive
as data, the loop emits this full lifecycle even for error/aborted turns —
one more reason persistence can hang off `message_end` alone. See [Prompt
lifecycle](07-lifecycle-and-hooks.qmd#sec:prompt-lifecycle) and [Agent
core](13-agent-core.qmd#sec:agent-core) for the full event ordering.

### Boundary 6 — `AgentMessage` → `SessionEntry` {#sec:boundary-6}

**Boundary 6 of 6 — `AgentMessage` → `SessionEntry`** (edge 6 in
@fig-type-chain).
*Type chain:* `SessionEntry` → `AgentMessage` → `Message` → `Context` →
wire payload → `AssistantMessageEvent` → **back to `SessionEntry`**.

`message_end` — the lifecycle event from Boundary 5 — is the persistence
trigger. `AgentSession` handles it (in `core/agent-session.ts`): ordinary
messages go to `SessionManager.appendMessage()`, extension-injected custom
messages to `appendCustomMessageEntry()`. Either way a new JSONL line is
appended as a child of the current leaf:

```ts
/** Append a message as child of current leaf, then advance leaf. Returns entry id.
 * Does not allow writing CompactionSummaryMessage and BranchSummaryMessage directly.
 * Reason: we want these to be top-level entries in the session, not message session entries,
 * so it is easier to find them.
 * These need to be appended via appendCompaction() and appendBranchSummary() methods.
 */
appendMessage(message: Message | CustomMessage | BashExecutionMessage): string;
```

`packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts`.
**Adds:** the `id` / `parentId` / `timestamp` envelope.
**Leaves behind:** nothing — the full record is kept.

The finished exchange closes the loop on disk — the summary message from our
running example lands with the same envelope shape you saw in [The same
message in three shapes](#sec:three-shapes) (`api`, `provider`, `model`, and
`usage` omitted as before; the `parentId` is the tool-result entry's id):

```json
{
  "type": "message",
  "id": "a42d91f0",
  "parentId": "5b6c7d8e",
  "timestamp": "2025-07-13T15:22:19.004Z",
  "message": {
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "README.md introduces the Pi ..." }
    ],
    "stopReason": "stop",
    "timestamp": 1752420139000
  }
}
```

Even a failed turn's assistant message is persisted (its `errorMessage` is
part of the record): failures are stream data, so the loop emits the full
`message_start`/`message_end` lifecycle for an error or aborted turn, and
the same `appendMessage()` path runs. `transformMessages()` then skips that
message when building the *next* request, so the model retries from the last
valid state while the file keeps a complete audit trail. One conversation,
back in its durable home — ready to be rebuilt into the next request.

## Why Pi has its own message representation {#sec:why-canonical}

This section answers question 1 from the intro.

::: {.callout-note}
## Skippable
This section explains why Pi owns a message format at all; the walk stands
alone without it. If you want the whole round trip in one picture first,
skip ahead to [The pipeline in one picture](#sec:pipeline-recap).
:::

You have now seen the two wire shapes at Boundary 4. So why doesn't Pi just
pick one — keep a provider's shape in its own three homes and pass it
straight through? Four reasons explain the architecture.

### Providers disagree about the basics

There is no standard for how a conversation is encoded. Two providers Pi
supports — chosen because they are the most common — already differ on the
fundamentals (you saw every row of this table at Boundary 4):

| Design question | OpenAI (Chat Completions) | Anthropic (Messages) |
|---|---|---|
| Tool-call arguments | JSON **string**, must be parsed | Structured `input` **object** |
| Tool result's role | Dedicated `tool` role | A `tool_result` block inside a **`user`** message |
| Result's key field | `tool_call_id` | `tool_use_id` |
| Streaming | Delta objects per chunk | Typed content-block events |
| Reasoning output | Model-specific fields | Signed `thinking` blocks |

If Pi's session file or agent loop spoke one provider's dialect, switching
models mid-session would corrupt the transcript — and Pi explicitly allows
switching (`/model`, and `model_change` entries in the session file). A
history stored as Anthropic `tool_use` blocks cannot be sent to OpenAI
as-is; a history stored as OpenAI `tool` messages cannot be sent to
Anthropic. Something in the middle must keep the conversation neutral.

### One hub, not a translator per pair

Pi supports ten chat provider APIs plus an image-generation API — one
adapter file each under `packages/ai/src/api/` — and dozens of provider
brands share those adapters. With a canonical hub format, adding a provider
means writing **one adapter**: canonical messages to wire JSON on the way
out, wire chunks to canonical events on the way in. Without the hub, every
feature that produces or consumes messages — the session store, compaction,
extension-injected messages, the TUI — would need its own converter per
provider. The hub turns an N×M problem — every feature that produces or
consumes messages, times every provider — into an N problem.

### The session file outlives provider APIs

A session file is a long-lived artifact: you can `/resume` a conversation
next week, branch it with `/tree` next month. Provider APIs, meanwhile,
version and deprecate constantly. If the durable record were provider JSON,
every provider migration would threaten every saved session. Keeping the
file in Pi's own format means provider changes are absorbed by one adapter
file, never by migrating your history.

### Each boundary drops information on purpose

The corollary of layered representations is that each conversion is
**one-directional and lossy by design**. Durable-only fields — extension
state, labels, thinking-level changes — never reach the provider, so they
never cost tokens or leak into someone else's logs. Provider quirks — ID
formats, role constraints — never leak back into the session file, so the
file stays valid for whichever model handles the next turn.

## The pipeline in one picture {#sec:pipeline-recap}

You have walked every boundary; @fig-representation-pipeline compresses the
round trip into one diagram. Trace each arrow against the boundary you just
read: follow the arrows left to right on the way out, right to left on the
way back. It is the process view of @fig-type-chain — same boundaries, same
functions, shown as participants exchanging messages rather than types
linked by edges.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-representation-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "One prompt's round trip through the representation pipeline. Outbound arrows (top) name the exact converting function; inbound arrows (bottom) carry the streamed response back to the session file. parseSessionEntries() is exported for compaction tests; the runtime load path is loadEntriesFromFile()."
%%| fig-width: 6.2
%%| fig-pos: "H"
sequenceDiagram
  participant F as session file<br/>(JSONL)
  participant S as SessionManager
  participant A as agent loop
  participant D as ai adapter
  participant P as provider
  F->>S: parseSessionEntries() → FileEntry[]
  S->>A: buildSessionContext() → AgentMessage[]
  A->>D: convertToLlm() → Context
  D->>D: transformMessages()
  D->>P: convertMessages() → provider JSON
  P->>D: SSE chunks → AssistantMessageEvent
  D->>A: stream done → AssistantMessage
  A->>S: message_end
  S->>F: appendMessage() → new JSONL line
```

Two labels deserve a gloss. A `FileEntry` is simply one file line: the
header or one `SessionEntry` — `parseSessionEntries()` returns `FileEntry[]`
because it reads the header too. And SSE is Server-Sent Events, the HTTP
convention of streaming a response as a series of text chunks.

## Choosing the right boundary {#sec:choose-boundary}

Each representation answers different questions. Work at the highest layer
that truthfully has the data you need (paths relative to `packages/` again):

| You want to... | Work with | See |
|---|---|---|
| Inspect or repair history, branches, or durable extension state | `SessionEntry` via `SessionManager`, in `core/session-manager.ts` | [Sessions, trees, and compaction](03-sessions-trees-compaction.qmd#sec:sessions) |
| Add a message kind the UI renders but the model may or may not see | `AgentMessage` via declaration merging, plus `convertToLlm`, in `core/messages.ts` | [Architecture](05-architecture-for-extensions.qmd#sec:architecture) |
| Change what the model sees per request (prune, inject) | `AgentMessage[]` in a `context` handler / `transformContext` | [Prompt lifecycle](07-lifecycle-and-hooks.qmd#sec:prompt-lifecycle), [Extension event reference](18-extension-event-reference.qmd#sec:events) |
| Change canonical message semantics for every consumer | `Message`, `Context`, in `ai/src/types.ts` | [Agent core](13-agent-core.qmd#sec:agent-core) |
| Inspect or replace the exact bytes sent to a provider | The wire payload via `before_provider_request` | [Models, providers, and authentication](12-models-providers-and-auth.qmd#sec:models) |
| Support a genuinely new wire protocol | A new adapter in `ai/src/api/` | [Guided source tours](17-guided-source-tours.qmd#sec:tours) |
| Render streaming output | `AssistantMessageEvent` via `message_update` | [Extension event reference](18-extension-event-reference.qmd#sec:events) |

Two rules of thumb cover most mistakes:

- **Durable state never crosses the provider boundary by accident.** If
  extension data must influence the model, inject it as a `custom_message`
  entry or a `context` handler; `pi.appendEntry()` alone keeps it private.
- **Provider JSON never leaks upward.** If you find yourself switching on
  `tool_calls` vs. `tool_use` outside `packages/ai/src/api/`, the logic
  belongs in an adapter.

## Beginner checkpoint

Name the representation and the converting function for each step:

1. A resumed session's file becomes the runtime transcript.
2. The transcript becomes the provider-neutral request messages.
3. Canonical messages become Anthropic's `tool_use`/`tool_result` JSON.
4. A streamed provider response becomes a persisted assistant message.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

1. `SessionEntry` lines to `AgentMessage[]`, via `buildSessionContext()`
   (parsing, branch walk, compaction, `sessionEntryToContextMessages()`).
2. `AgentMessage[]` to `Message[]` inside a `Context`, via the coding-agent
   `convertToLlm()` in `core/messages.ts`.
3. `Message[]` to wire JSON, via `transformMessages()` then the adapter's
   `convertMessages()` in `packages/ai/src/api/anthropic-messages.ts`.
4. Provider chunks to `AssistantMessageEvent`s on an
   `AssistantMessageEventStream`, then `message_end` triggers
   `SessionManager.appendMessage()` — a new JSONL `message` entry.

If you can place each conversion in its owning package, the pipeline is
working.
:::

Continue to [Prompt
lifecycle](07-lifecycle-and-hooks.qmd#sec:prompt-lifecycle) for a
stage-by-stage trace of one prompt through the events and hooks that surround
this pipeline.
